questions.title: Duration of the indifferent gonad stage
questions.question: The sex gland is called "the indifferent gonad" until the:

explanations.A: Correct. The early gonad forms from the genital ridge as a sexually undifferentiated (indifferent) structure with both a cortex and a medulla. It remains morphologically identical in male and female embryos until about the 7th week, when the SRY gene (in the presence of a Y chromosome) drives medullary development into a testis, and in its absence the cortex develops into an ovary a little later. Before the 7th week the gonad cannot be told apart histologically as male or female.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By the 9th week sexual differentiation of the gonad has already begun; the indifferent stage ends earlier, around the 7th week.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The 12th week is far too late; testicular cords and early ovarian differentiation are established well before this.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By the 15th week the external genitalia are also differentiating; the gonad is long past its indifferent stage.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: State that the gonad remains indifferent until about the 7th week, when sexual differentiation begins.

questions.title: Funnel-shaped lateral end of the fallopian tube
questions.question: The lateral funnel shaped end of the fallopian tube is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The isthmus is the narrow, thick-walled medial third of the tube next to the uterus, not a funnel.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The intramural (interstitial) part is the short segment passing through the uterine wall, the narrowest portion of the tube.
explanations.C: Correct. The uterine (fallopian) tube ends laterally in the infundibulum, a trumpet- or funnel-shaped expansion that opens into the peritoneal cavity through the abdominal ostium. Its margin bears finger-like fimbriae that sweep over the ovary and guide the ovulated oocyte into the tube. This funnel shape distinguishes it from the tubular ampulla, isthmus and intramural parts.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ampulla is the wide, thin-walled, tortuous middle segment where fertilisation usually occurs, but it is tubular rather than funnel-shaped.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: Identify the infundibulum as the funnel-shaped lateral end of the uterine tube.

questions.title: Adult growth-hormone-secreting tumour (acromegaly)
questions.question: A 34-year-old woman who develops a growth-hormone-secreting tumour:

options.A: May increase in length to reach 2 metres or more.
options.B: Has decreased secretion of 4-hydroxyproline in the urine.
options.C: Will likely have to buy a larger pair of shoes than those used before the disease started.

explanations.A: Incorrect. In an adult the epiphyseal plates are already fused, so linear (long-bone) growth cannot resume; gigantism only occurs when excess growth hormone acts before epiphyseal closure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Growth hormone stimulates collagen turnover, so urinary hydroxyproline is increased, not decreased.
explanations.C: Correct. After epiphyseal fusion, excess growth hormone causes acromegaly: appositional periosteal bone growth and soft-tissue overgrowth thicken and enlarge the acral parts (hands, feet, jaw and face). The feet broaden, so the patient characteristically needs progressively larger shoes and gloves. This acral enlargement, not increased height, is the hallmark of adult growth-hormone excess.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Growth hormone is a counter-regulatory, diabetogenic hormone; it raises blood glucose and tends to cause hyperglycaemia, not hypoglycaemia.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Recognise acromegaly (acral enlargement, larger shoe size) as the result of growth-hormone excess after epiphyseal fusion.

questions.title: High TSH with low T4
questions.question: A patient has high TSH and low T4. This is diagnosed as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Secondary hypothyroidism is due to pituitary failure, so TSH would be low (or inappropriately normal) together with the low T4, not high.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism shows a high T4; primary hyperthyroidism additionally suppresses TSH to low levels.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The posterior pituitary secretes ADH and oxytocin, not TSH, so a posterior pituitary lesion does not produce this thyroid pattern.
explanations.D: Correct. In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid gland itself fails, so T4 falls. The reduced negative feedback on the anterior pituitary releases it from inhibition, so TSH rises. The combination of a high TSH with a low T4 therefore localises the defect to the gland (primary hypothyroidism).

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Interpret a high TSH with a low T4 as primary hypothyroidism.

questions.title: Hypocalcaemia and tetany after thyroid surgery
questions.question: A patient presents with hypocalcaemia and tetany after thyroid surgery. What is the expected cause?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperthyroidism does not cause hypocalcaemic tetany; if anything thyroid hormone excess tends to raise, not lower, plasma calcium.
explanations.B: Correct. The parathyroid glands lie against the posterior surface of the thyroid, so thyroidectomy can inadvertently remove or devascularise them. Loss of parathyroid hormone removes the main defence against a falling plasma calcium, so ionised calcium drops. The resulting hypocalcaemia increases neuromuscular excitability and produces tetany (carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vitamin D excess raises intestinal calcium absorption and causes hypercalcaemia, the opposite of this picture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although calcitonin lowers calcium, physiological or even tumour calcitonin excess rarely produces symptomatic hypocalcaemia; the temporal link to thyroid surgery points to parathyroid loss.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Attribute post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemic tetany to inadvertent parathyroid removal.

questions.title: Expected finding in Addison's disease
questions.question: In Addison's disease, one would expect:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Addison's disease is primary adrenocortical failure, so cortisol levels are low, not high.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Aldosterone deficiency causes sodium and water loss with hypovolaemia, producing hypotension rather than hypertension.
explanations.C: Correct. Cortisol is a counter-regulatory hormone that supports blood glucose by promoting gluconeogenesis and opposing insulin. In Addison's disease cortisol deficiency impairs gluconeogenesis, so patients are prone to fasting hypoglycaemia. This is compounded by anorexia and poor intake.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Low cortisol removes feedback on the pituitary, raising ACTH (and its melanocyte-stimulating precursor POMC), which causes hyperpigmentation, not hypopigmentation.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Recognise hypoglycaemia as an expected consequence of cortisol deficiency in Addison's disease.

questions.title: Why T3 is more active than T4
questions.question: T3 is more active than T4 because:

options.B: It has higher affinity to receptors.
options.C: It is more bound to plasma proteins.

explanations.A: Incorrect. T4 is actually the more abundant secretory product of the thyroid; T3 is present in smaller amounts, much of it formed peripherally by deiodination of T4.
explanations.B: Correct. T3 binds the nuclear thyroid-hormone receptor with roughly ten times the affinity of T4, so it drives gene transcription far more effectively. Because the receptor is what mediates thyroid-hormone action, this higher receptor affinity makes T3 the metabolically more potent (active) hormone. T4 largely serves as a circulating prohormone that is converted to T3 in the tissues.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T3 is in fact less tightly bound to plasma proteins than T4; greater protein binding would reduce, not increase, the active free fraction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T4 has the longer plasma half-life and larger stored/bound pool; longer storage does not explain the greater biological activity of T3.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Explain that T3 is more active than T4 because of its higher affinity for the nuclear thyroid-hormone receptor.

questions.title: Feature NOT produced by excess thyroid hormone
questions.question: A tumour secreting excess T3 and T4 does NOT produce:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Thyroid hormone excess up-regulates cardiac beta-adrenergic responsiveness, so tachycardia is a typical feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The raised metabolic rate increases heat production and cutaneous vasodilation and sweating, giving warm, flushed, moist skin.
explanations.C: Correct. Thyroid hormone raises the basal metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, which increases the respiratory drive; hyperthyroid patients therefore breathe faster (tachypnoea), often with exertional dyspnoea. Bradypnoea (abnormally slow breathing) is the opposite and is not a feature of thyrotoxicosis. It is the one option that excess T3/T4 does not produce.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hypermetabolic state increases energy expenditure and, despite a good appetite, leads to weight loss.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Identify bradypnoea as the feature NOT caused by thyroid-hormone excess (which causes tachypnoea).

questions.title: Insulin and IGF-1 share a receptor
questions.question: Regarding insulin hormone, which statement is correct?

options.A: Insulin release from beta cells is decreased by inactivating ATP-sensitive K+ channels.
options.C: Insulin facilitates glucose entry into the renal tubules by increasing the number of GLUT4.
options.D: Insulin and IGF-1 can bind to the same receptor.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Closing (inactivating) the ATP-sensitive K+ channel depolarises the beta cell and increases insulin release; it does not decrease it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leptin inhibits insulin secretion (the adipo-insular axis); it does not stimulate it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Renal tubular glucose handling uses insulin-independent transporters (SGLT and GLUT2); insulin does not recruit GLUT4 into renal tubular cells.
explanations.D: Correct. Insulin and insulin-like growth factor-1 are structurally homologous, and their receptors are closely related tyrosine-kinase receptors. Because of this homology the two ligands show cross-reactivity, and insulin can bind and weakly activate the IGF-1 receptor (and vice versa). This shared, overlapping receptor binding underlies some of the growth-promoting actions seen when insulin is present at high concentrations.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: State that insulin and IGF-1 are homologous and can cross-bind each other's receptors.

questions.title: Fruity breath with deep rapid breathing
questions.question: An unconscious patient has rapid deep breathing and a fruity breath odour. The most likely explanation is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hypercalcaemia causes lethargy, constipation and polyuria, not Kussmaul breathing or a fruity odour.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypoglycaemia causes sweating, tremor and altered consciousness, but not deep sighing respiration or ketotic breath.
explanations.C: Correct. In diabetic ketoacidosis, insulin lack drives lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, producing acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. The metabolic acidosis stimulates deep, rapid Kussmaul respiration to blow off CO2, and the volatile acetone gives the breath its characteristic fruity odour. This combination in an unconscious patient points to ketoacidosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adrenal (Addisonian) crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia and shock rather than Kussmaul breathing with a fruity smell.

questions.subject: endo
questions.learning_objective: Recognise Kussmaul breathing with a fruity (acetone) odour as a sign of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.title: Hormone deficient in the anaemia of chronic kidney disease
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops anaemia. Which hormone is deficient?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Calcitonin is a thyroid C-cell hormone that lowers plasma calcium; it has no role in red-cell production.
explanations.B: Correct. Erythropoietin is a glycoprotein hormone produced mainly by peritubular interstitial (fibroblast-like) cells of the renal cortex in response to hypoxia. It stimulates erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow to proliferate and mature. In chronic kidney disease the loss of functioning renal tissue reduces erythropoietin output, so red-cell production falls and a normocytic normochromic anaemia develops.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cortisol is an adrenocortical glucocorticoid; its deficiency causes Addison's disease, not the anaemia specific to renal failure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Insulin is a pancreatic hormone regulating glucose metabolism and is not responsible for the anaemia of kidney disease.

questions.subject: renal
questions.learning_objective: Attribute the anaemia of chronic kidney disease to deficient renal erythropoietin.

questions.title: Hormone secreted by theca interna cells
questions.question: Theca interna cells secrete which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The theca interna does not make estrogen directly; estrogen is produced by the granulosa cells, which aromatise theca-derived androgens.
explanations.B: Correct. Under the influence of LH, the theca interna cells synthesise androgens, chiefly androstenedione, from cholesterol. This androstenedione then diffuses to the neighbouring granulosa cells, where FSH-induced aromatase converts it to estradiol. The theca interna therefore provides the androgen substrate in the two-cell, two-gonadotropin model of ovarian estrogen synthesis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. FSH is a gonadotropin secreted by the anterior pituitary, not by ovarian follicular cells.
explanations.D: Incorrect. LH is also an anterior pituitary gonadotropin; it acts on the theca interna but is not secreted by it.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: State that theca interna cells secrete androstenedione, the substrate for granulosa-cell estrogen synthesis.

questions.title: Histological classification of the mammary gland
questions.question: The mammary gland is classified as being a:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mammary gland has a branching duct system draining many lobules, so it is compound (not simple branched) and its secretory units are tubuloalveolar rather than purely alveolar.
explanations.B: Correct. The mammary gland is a compound gland: multiple lobules of secretory tubuloalveolar units drain through a branching duct system to the nipple. Its secretory mode is classically described as apocrine for the lipid component, in which the apical cytoplasm containing the fat droplet is pinched off with the secretion. This makes it a compound tubuloalveolar apocrine gland.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Holocrine secretion (whole-cell disintegration, as in sebaceous glands) does not describe the mammary gland.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Although the protein (milk) component is released by merocrine exocytosis, the gland's characteristic classification includes its apocrine lipid secretion, so "merocrine" alone is not the intended answer.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: Classify the mammary gland as a compound tubuloalveolar apocrine gland.

questions.title: Characteristic of Cowper's (bulbourethral) glands
questions.question: Cowper's glands are characterised by:

options.B: Their duct joining the membranous part of the urethra.
options.C: They neutralise any traces of acidic urine.
options.D: Their secretion is rich in fibrinolysin.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The bulk of seminal fluid (about 60-70%) comes from the seminal vesicles; the bulbourethral glands contribute only a small pre-ejaculatory amount.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cowper's glands lie in the deep perineal pouch, but their ducts open into the bulbous (penile/spongy) part of the urethra, not the membranous part.
explanations.C: Correct. The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands are small mucous glands whose clear, alkaline, slippery secretion is released into the urethra ahead of the semen. This alkaline mucus lubricates the urethra and neutralises residual acidic urine, protecting the spermatozoa that follow. Cleaning and buffering the urethral lumen is their characteristic role.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fibrinolysin, which reliquefies coagulated semen, is a prostatic product, not a bulbourethral one.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: State that Cowper's (bulbourethral) gland secretion lubricates and neutralises acidic urine in the urethra.

questions.title: Function of the oviduct peg cells
questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding peg cells?

options.A: Help in capacitation of the spermatozoa.
options.C: Progesterone decreases their number during the secretory phase.
options.D: Beat and push the ovum towards the uterus.

explanations.A: Correct. Peg cells are the non-ciliated, secretory cells of the uterine-tube epithelium, wedged between the ciliated cells. Their secretion forms the tubal fluid that nourishes the oocyte and early embryo and contributes to sperm capacitation, the final maturation that enables spermatozoa to fertilise. Thus peg cells help capacitate the spermatozoa.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Relaxin is produced by the corpus luteum and placenta, not by tubal peg cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Progesterone in the luteal (secretory) phase increases secretory (peg) cell activity; it does not reduce their number.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Beating to move the ovum is the job of the ciliated cells; peg cells are secretory and non-ciliated.

questions.subject: gyn
questions.learning_objective: State that the secretory peg cells of the uterine tube aid sperm capacitation.

questions.title: Genital duct with a three-layered muscular coat
questions.question: One of the following has a musculosa arranged into 3 layers:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tubuli recti (straight tubules) are short intratesticular channels lined by Sertoli-like cells with only sparse surrounding tissue, not a three-layered muscle coat.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ejaculatory duct has a thin fibromuscular wall and lacks the thick trilaminar muscular coat of the vas.
explanations.C: Correct. The vas (ductus) deferens has a characteristically thick muscular wall arranged in three layers: an inner longitudinal, a middle circular, and an outer longitudinal layer of smooth muscle. This powerful musculature produces the peristaltic contractions that propel spermatozoa during emission. Its thick trilaminar musculosa around a narrow, folded lumen is a hallmark identifying feature.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The rete testis is a network of channels in the mediastinum testis lined by simple epithelium, without a three-layered muscular coat.

questions.subject: androl
questions.learning_objective: Identify the vas deferens as the genital duct with a three-layered (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal) muscular coat.
